texto: It is a cold night in November. You are reading by
the lamp, and something starts buzzing around the shade.
A brown, shield-shaped bug. It flies like a drunk helicopter,
bonks into the lamp, and lands on your sleeve.
Your first thought is to squish it, or flush it.
But what if you just let it be? What happens to a stink
bug that spends the whole winter in your house?
The short answer is, almost nothing.
And that is the strange part.
This is the brown marmorated stink bug.
Look for the little white bands on its antennae and legs.
It is not from here. It comes from East Asia.
The first ones in America were collected in Allentown, Pennsylvania, in
nineteen ninety-eight. Probably stowaways in a shipping container.
Today they live in as many as forty-seven
states.
Every fall, when the nights get cold, they go looking for a place to spend the winter.
And a warm house, full of tiny gaps
around windows, doors and air conditioners, is perfect.
Once a few find a good spot, they give
off a chemical signal that invites their friends.
One man in Maryland collected every stink bug he found inside his home,
every single day, for six months.
His final count was more than twenty-six thousand.
In one house.
So what do they do in there? Mostly, they sleep.
They tuck themselves into wall spaces, attics and behind
the siding, and slip into a deep winter rest called
diapause. They do not eat your food.
They do not mate. They do not lay eggs. They do not chew your house.
It is like having a roommate who pays no rent,
never cooks, never talks, and sleeps from
Halloween to Easter.
The trouble starts on warm days. When the sun heats the walls,
or the furnace runs, some of them wake up,
confused, and wander out into your rooms.
The Maryland study found the same thing.
More bugs came out on days that were warmer than normal.
So they buzz toward your lamps and windows, slow and clumsy,
because their bodies still think it is winter.
Inside a dry, heated house, many of them simply run out of energy.
They are found on windowsills in
spring. And then there is the smell.
Squeeze one, and it sprays a defensive chemical from
glands on its body. Here is the weird part.
One of those chemicals is the same one that gives cilantro its smell.
So if cilantro tastes like soap to you,
this bug is your worst nightmare.
It cannot bite and it cannot sting. But the spray can irritate some people,
and make a curious dog drool.
When spring arrives, the survivors climb toward the light, and head
back outside to mate. And this is where the story turns.
Outside, this bug feeds on more than
a hundred kinds of crops. Apples, peaches, tomatoes,
peppers, sweet corn. In twenty ten,
it damaged an estimated thirty-seven million dollars' worth of
apples in the mid-Atlantic alone.
Scientists have a hope, though. A tiny wasp from Asia,
called the samurai wasp, that lays its eggs inside stink bug
eggs. So what should you do with the one
on your sleeve? Do not squish it.
Grab a jar with some soapy water, and nudge the bug in. It cannot climb out.
For a crowd, try the trick from Virginia Tech.
A pan of soapy water under a lamp,
in a dark room, at night. And before next September,
seal the gaps around your windows, doors
and air conditioner.
So what happens if you let a stink bug live in your house all winter?
It sleeps. It wakes up confused.
And in spring, it leaves to go eat your neighbor's peaches.
The perfect roommate. Until it
moves out.
